speechtext:
Or to rubber stamp your
will.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That might be. What,
sir, is the duty of this party? The duty of

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
every man in this house is to think in terms of his country, and when he finds in 1923 the Prime Minister declaiming against a possible attitude of mind towards the great republic to the south in dealing with fiscal matters, and then changing his mind and calling upon his friend from Brandon and that gentleman's associates to support reductions in the tariff from year to year,-I say the duty of every hon. member is clear. We who criticize know that the right hon. gentleman does not change his mind so lightly, we know there is a purpose behind the change, and we have a right to seek the purpose. And if we have a right to point out the effect we have also a right to point out the purpose. The purpose is power; the effect is injury to Canada. It means loss of population to this country. And it means more than that. The American commercial reports indicating the movement of farm machinery to this country mean that just so many Canadians as might have been engaged in the manufacture of that machinery here are without jobs. Is it treason to point that out? Did the right hon. gentleman hesitate to do it when he talked of usurpation of power and abuse of the institutions of this country? When he spoke of those matters in days gone by was it treason on his part? Do hon. gentlemen opposite fancy that they can becloud the minds of the Canadian people by making such observations? Let me assure them that so long as we are here, so long as we occupy the seats to which we have been elected, we propose fearlessly to criticize the acts of the government notwithstanding what they may say. It ill becomes ministers of the crown, responsible ministers, to foster such a delusion as that and to charge us with engaging in immigration propaganda in the interests of the United States. My hon. friends opposite know perfectly well that people are shut out of that country under the laws that prevail there. Aware of these things, we propose to criticize the government so long as no effort is made to provide work for our people; because work is what is very urgently needed in Canada. Every effort, therefore, which this party makes is an effort to secure work for Canadians and not for others.
I would remind my hon. friends of one other fact. When they were in opposition what did they do? They were not content to make speeches on subjects such as my hon. friend from Hants-Kings has discussed; they moved resolutions. And what was the purport if the resolutions they moved in 1889, in 1890 ind again in 1891? It was to secure unrestricted freedom in the trade relations uetween the United States and Canada. The 
reform which was suggested, to quote the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was the absolute reciprocal freedom of trade between the two countries. This briefly sums up the history of my hon. friends in this regard; this is the record of those who now attack us because we venture to assert the rights of Canada and to urge those rights as being of greater moment to us than the interests of the United States. When we turn to the record of the party opposite when in opposition, we find that, making a strong appeal for support in 1891, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
The reform suggested by the Liberal party is absolute reciprocal freedom of trade between Canada and the United States.
How long would there have been a Dominion of Canada had that policy been carried into effect? Is that my hon. friends' policy to-day? Is that the goal towards which they are striving? Is that the reason for the tariff being reduced? Is that the reason that they are pursuing the course proposed in days gone by? Let my hon. friends answer these questions before they attack those who sit to the left of the Speaker.
I will not venture to trespass further on the time of the house, but I merely point out that, according to the Commercial Intelligence Journal which we received last week,
I find at page 354 that whereas the imports of automobile parts for assembly amounted in 1927 to $29,582,000, in 1926 they were only $25,000,000, an increase of over $4,000,000; while automobile parts for replacement are given respectively as $4,919,000 and $3,600,000. The same condition of things exists in regard to rods. That is the effect of the government s legislation:	with decreasing exports we are assembling parts to a greater extent than before. This means less work for Canadians-less manufacturing and an increasing tendency towards the assembling of parts. Now, what is the aim of the Conservative party? It is to endeavour to make this country economically independent. Our objective is to render the Dominion of Canada no longer dependent upon foreigners for our economic existence. I put this to the government:	If we are obliged always to
go abroad for all our machinery, what will happen supposing, in a moment of caprice, that foreign supply is shut off? What did Adam Smith say on this point?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely you will not
quote him.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I admit that one should be reluctant to quote Adam Smith after the Prime Minister, but I do not think it is at

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
all amiss to point out the ground on which Adam Smith justified the taking care of industry at home. I ask this house quite seriously this question:	is this country to
become economically a dependent or an independent community? Are we to find ourselves in such a situation that, at the caprice of a powerful neighbour, for purposes solely selfish and entirely in its own interests, we shall be excluded from our sources of supply? Yet this has happened before. Do my hon. friends realize that in Europe one country has established, and to-day maintains at an annual loss, a factory for the purpose of ensuring that its people shall not be dependent upon foreign supplies as they were during the war? Do hon. gentlemen realize that this particular industry now operates in the Netherlands? Well, is Canada going to find itself in a similar predicament? All we endeavour to do, Mr. Speaker, is by every legislative means within our power, to use the words of a great Englishman, and with the tools that are in our hands, whether they be tariffs, regulations, bonuses, drawbacks, or bounties, to bend our efforts to one purpose and one purpose only, namely, to make the Canadian people a strong and virile nation, developing their own resources to the limit of their ability, and thus become entirely economically independent of foreigners, whoever they may be or wherever they may be found
I have not the time this afternoon to dwell upon the trade treaties which have been entered into by this government; I cannot indicate the extent to which the government has failed in respect of these agreements. Suffice it to say that every trade treaty which the government has entered into has operated against the Dominion of Canada. There is, perhaps, one exception respecting which there may be some doubt; I refer to the treaty with the Netherlands. But so far as the others are concerned I think the statement I have just made can be accepted without any qualification. We have made treaties with Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Italy and France.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And South Africa.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and South Africa. And all these treaties have been equally disastrous to Canada. See what happened but yesterday: France raised its duties but we were powerless. We cannot touch ours unless we abrogate the treaty; so the minister told me yesterday. In Australia they increased their tariff; we are powerless. Why? Simply because we were not skilful enough as bargainers; they outreached us; they outgeneraled us. The bargain, so far as they
are concerned, leaves them free to raise their tariff against us while, without abrogating the treaty, we are powerless to touch our tariff as it affects them. Did my hon. friends know that? Do they know that we cannot touch these items without cancelling the treaties we have with these countries? The Minister of Finance was waited upon the other day by a certain delegation-this will reveal his state of mind concerning these treaties-and when he heard a complaint regarding certain items in the schedules affected he remarked, "You did not support me properly with respect to the Australian treaty". It appears, then, that industry is to be punished if it fails to support the Minister of Finance. Is that the law of this country? Is that the way in which Canada is to be governed? If so, clearly our tariff is but a political tariff. Legislation has been introduced, retroactive in its character, for one purpose and one purpose only, and I say that such a thing is improper. It is improper for the Minister of Finance to tell certain people that inasmuch as they did not support his Australian treaty to his satisfaction he will do nothing for them. This, I submit, is anything but a proper frame of mind for the Minister of Finance, whoever he may be; it is not the right attitude for any Canadian minister to take towards the industrial life of the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have moved an amendment the affirmative of which we say clearly expresses the attitude of the party to which we belong. Our position is stated in simple, clearcut language. In order that there may no misunderstanding, let me once more read that amendment:
This house regrets that the measures proposed by the government do not tend to provide increased employment in Canada nor to induce the return of Canadians to their native land, nor to prevent the continued emigration of our people to the United States; and that they make no provisions for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products. nor for the effective development of the natural resources of the country, nor for the abolition of the sales tax by the first of January 1929.
The policy of the Conservative party is to increase employment in Canada, to keep our people here and to induce the return of Canadians to their native land. The evidence given before this high court of parliament by the hon. members who have taken part in this debate proves conclusively that the policies in force at present are not having this effect, and neither are they preventing the continued emigration of our people to the United States.
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

The amendment also expresses regret that no provision has been made for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products. I have under my hand a letter dealing with the butter and egg situation; the last commercial report deals with the competition of Russia in the egg markets of Great Britain. Look at our imports of butter and eggs and dairy products and see our position with respect to these matters. No attempt is made in the budget to improve that condition. Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) tried to give some of the dairy interests of Canada a little comfort by quietly suggesting that the Australian treaty was not inviolable, but that there was provision by which it might be abrogated. Did he consult the Minister of Finance as to whether or not he would abrogate it? Not yet. That is the way in which the government is conducted, to try and induce hon. members yonder to believe the treaty will be abrogated in order that they may vote properly, while the Minister of Finance sits quietly in his seat knowing very well that he has no intention of abrogating that treaty in any way. In other words, if I might be permitted to use a colloquialism, it is his own baby and he proposes to nourish it. The amendment also regrets that no provision is made for the effective development of the natural resources of the country. You Only have to consider the American commerce reports and the other publications to which I have alluded, to make the position perfectly clear.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the affirmative of that amendment expresses our settled convictions.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But not your policy.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It also expresses our
policy, as outlined at Winnipeg. There is high authority for saying the policy is a chart, and there is still higher authority for saying it was never a compass, as far as the hon. gentleman is concerned. He feels very much hurt that he will no longer be able to make his diatribes against the Conservative party because of their alleged position with respect to tariff policies. Now he and the Minister of Agriculture must face the electors of Saskatchewan and explain why the butter markets of this country are being destroyed and why the farmers of Saskatchewan are going out of the dairying business. They will also have to explain why 3,000 head of dairy cattle were sold in Colchester county alone in the last six months.
These things will have to be explained, and the policy to which I have alluded is the policy of the party with which I have the honour to

be associated for the present. We have no apologies to offer; we stand four-square by that policy, and repeat that Canada can only be built up by a proper appreciation of all those principles which political economists say are essential to the development of the resources of a new land. We must practise economy; we must practise thrift; we must reduce our national debt as rapidly as possible, to maintain the great heritage which Providence has given to us. In the words of the Prime Minister himself, this can only be done by taking full cognizance of the fact that there is a great republic to the south clamouring for our markets, invading them at every point and securing them wherever possible. Every bit of legislative machinery in our power and every tool we can pick up must be taken in hand and used to effect the purpose we have in mind, and when that purpose is effected they may be laid down again. If the country is being exploited by industry then this country and this parliament can deal with it.

Now, sir, I have trespassed upon the time and attention of this house very much longer than I had intended, but there were many matters which came to my mind and which I thought should be dealt with. I am conscious of not having dealt with as many of them as I should have liked, but I do commend to this house and to this country the thought that in so far as we are endeavouring to criticize fearlessly, boldly and courageously the proposals of the government, we are within our rights. Every effort we can make to secure the health, happiness and prosperity of the people of this country will be made, and we will continue to urge that economy be practised in the conduct of our national affairs in order that we may no longer be threatened with the economic menace to which the president of the United States so fittingly referred.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening his remarks my friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) expressed his appreciation of the high character and tone of the debate which has now lasted for almost four weeks. I am happy to join with him in his apprecia-

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
tion of the speeches which have been delivered. May I also venture to congratulate him on having the front rows of the opposition benches filled for the first time since this parliament has been in session. He has succeeded in bringing his wanderers back from different parts of the world. I see my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who has just returned to us from the West Indies; my friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who has just returned from Great Britain, and my friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), who has also come back from across the ocean. I say to these hon. members that we are pleased to see them here and glad to see them looking so hale and hearty. I might also say that I imagine not one of them has read the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). I doubt if they have read the amendments which have been moved by the Conservative party and the Progressive group; on the other hand I venture the assurance that they will all vote for the amendment proposed by the opposition, that they will vote against the amendment of the Progressive group and against the budget.
May I say to my hon. friend that I appreciate the manner of his presentation of the point of view of the opposition in its criticism of the budget. I shall endeavour to follow him as well as I can in the order in which he proceeded, and try to touch upon the various subjects with which he dealt. He opened his remarks by a number of references to hon. gentlemen on this side of the house who have spoken during the course of the debate. Most of those references were in the nature of poetic effusions-I do not know that I can follow my hon. friend there. One little quotation, however, did come to my mind, as I listened while he lectured us, and told of what had been done elsewhere as well as what should be done here. As I watched the expression on the faces of those who surround him, I thought of those lines:
And still they gazed and still the wonder grew,
That one small head should carry all he knew.
As far as I was able to follow my hon. friend, he began with references to the public debt. From that he proceeded to a discussion of railway finance, then he dealt with the taxation which is proposed for the coming year. He came next to the tariff and spoke at some length in that connection. Finally he concluded by a reference to the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), which he said he was going to read to the house. Unfortunately,
however, my hon. friend did not read the amendment, and for the sake of those members of his party who have just returned perhaps I could not do better than read it in order that they may know exactly what it is they are expected to support.
First of all, what is the present position? The Minister of Finance made a motion to the effect that the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means to consider certain resolutions which he was anxious to present. These resolutions are in accord with similar resolutions which have been moved by the Minister of Finance in previous years. They agree with those resolutions in following lines of fiscal policy which have been consistently maintained by the government from the very day that we took office, and which have brought surpluses instead of deficits, reductions instead of increases in public debt, and reductions instead of increases in taxation. My hon. friend in presenting his motion gave to the house a statement of the finances of the country during the past year. But my hon. friend the leader of the opposition seems to think that the Finance minister should not have touched upon the past year, and rather chided him with having failed to say a little more about the year to come. The Minister of Finance was erring on the safe side when, in giving a statement of the government's policies with respect to taxation and tariff and how they had worked out in the past year, he indicated that in following similar" lines for the coming year, he was safe in predicting that the statement he would present at the end of the next financial year would be similar to that which he was then presenting. What was that statement? It was a statement to the effect that the balance sheet of the country showed a surplus, a very large surplus, a surplus running into very many millions of dollars; that it showed reductions in the public debt of many millions, and reductions in taxation as well. Those were the three outstanding features of the budget. The Minister of Finance pointed out wherein, by following along lines he indicated, the government had been able to achieve these results, and he predicted that in the next statement which he would present, following lines parallel to those Which had been followed in the past year, there would be another surplus, further reduction of the pubic debt, and possibly further reductions of taxation. One would have thought that the presentation of a statement of that character would have met with some measure of general appreciation. Instead of that, however, it has brought forth two amendments, each of which is similar to the other in one

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
particular only, namely, that each is in the nature of an expression of regret that the Minister of Finance has not gone far enough. But the interesting feature of the two amendments is this-that while hon. gentlemen immediately opposite regret that the Minister of Finance has not gone far enough in one direction, the Progressive group are supporting an amendment which regrets that the government has not gone further in an opposite direction. That is the real significance of the two amendments which are 'before us. Let me read the amendments in the words in which they have been presented to the house.
On February 16 the Minister of Finance moved:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
On February 20, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George moved the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
This house regrets that the measures proposed by the government do not tend to provide increased employment in Canada, nor to induce the return of Canadians to their native land, nor to prevent the continued emigration of our people to the United States; and that they make no provisions for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products, nor for the effective development of the natural resources of the country, nor for the abolition of the sales tax by the 1st of January, 1929.
Then on February 22nd, the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Fansher), of the Progressive group, moved:
.	ah the words after the word "regrets"
in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"That the government proposes further reductions in the income tax, thus making a serious departure from the principle of direct taxation; that the proposed revision of the customs tariff is inadequate to bring effective re let to the consuming public; and that the sales tax on the necessaries of life has not been eliminated.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, these amendments are similar in one particular only, namely, that each expresses a certain regret. It is true that each takes cognizance of the salles tax. Hon. gentlemen immediately opposite regret that the sales tax was not completely removed. Hon. gentlemen supporting the subamendment regret that the tax is not wholly removed on the necessaries of life. But when it comes to the rest of the amendments, hon. gentlemen of both parties regret that we have not followed policies based on fiscal principles diametrically opposed to one another. That is the line of criticism that the government

has to meet. The public, I think, will be quick to appreciate that those who are opposing the government are greatly divided and not united. The public will be able to make a comparison between the weakness of the disunited criticism of the opposition and the merit of the united support which the budget will receive from this side of the house.
Let me come immediately to the question of the public debt. In order that the policy of the present administration may be appreciated in its true perspective, it is necessary to consider the situation as the government encountered it when we came into office. My hon. friend, in the course of his remarks, gave certain figures of taxation during the six or eight years prior to that time. He pointed out that during that period the governments then in office had taken from the taxpayers of Canada only a certain amount of taxation. He then quoted the amounts which had been taken from the taxpayers since we came into office and said:	"Behold the
much greater amount of taxation which the present government has taken from the people of this Dominion." Rightly understood, my ihon. friend's comparison is a condemnation of hon. gentlemen opposite. What took place during the eight or ten years which preceded our coming into office? When the country was at war did hon. gentlemen opposite tax the people of Canada as was done in England, in France, anl elsewhere in order to carry on the war? They did not tax them to the extent of a single dollar for the purpose of carrying on the war, but left to their successors the payment of every dollar of the capital cost of the war. They did worse than that. They left to their successors the payment as well of every dollar of the cost of demobilization. My hon. friend talked about the mortgage on the farm. His friends left the country with a mortgage to the extent of one billion and several hundreds of millions of dollars, not one dollar of which did they seek to meet while in office. When we came into power we were at once confronted with the debts left by hon. gentlemen apposite. We found that the country had been going deeper and deeper into debt, and we took the first step necessary to save it, namely, that of seeking to "make ends meet," or in other words, to balance the budget. May I go further. Hon. gentlemen may say with respect to the war that the expenditure was abnormal, and that they did not expect to be able to meet that expenditure by taxation at the time. But what about the normal, ordinary expenditures at the time they were in office? If my memory

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
serves me aright, hon. gentlemen opposite, when they say they were taxing the people so lightly, added in the period of the war and demobilization on ordinary account an expenditure of something over $13,773,000. To this was added another $173,000,000 of deficits for the fiscal years 1920-21, 1921-22. That is the situation with which we were confronted. What did the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, point out? He informed parliament that if the policy continued of not balancing the budget, of not even seeking to have revenues equal expenditures, this country would go further and further into bankruptcy and from bankruptcy into utter ruin. It was to overcome that situation and to reach a point where our finances would be on an even basis that this government undertook to levy a little more in the way of additional taxation, sufficient to help to reach a point where expenditures and revenues would be more or less equal. We came into office on December 29,1921. That was the fiscal year for which hon. gentlemen opposite had provided. Their own Minister of Finance prepared the budget, and I claim, and I think hon. gentlemen will admit, that the figures relating to that year belong appropriately to their administration. I will say for my hon. friend's predecessor that he had courage enough to add something in the way of taxation during the time that he was in office. He had greater courage in that regard than the Union government which preceded him, but he did not add anything like enough to meet even the expenditures which he incurred, as I will show in a few moments. But if you compare the two years of his administration with the three following years of our administration, which three years were taken to bring about an adjustment of the finances of Canada, a readjustment so that we would reach a point at which the budget would balance, and then the three yjears following, you will see the successful working out of a consistent line of policy on the part of the Liberal administration. Those years disclose what? They disclose, as the Minister of Finance showed in the budget statement which he made the other day, surpluses instead of deficits, reduction of debt instead of increase of debt, reduction of taxation instead of increase of taxation. Let me give the statement to the house as briefly as I can.
According to the public accounts for the fiscal year 1920-21-1 am giving the figures in millions of dollars-the total revenue amounted to $436,000,000 and the expenditure to $528,000,000, or a deficit of $92,000,000. That deficit of $92,000,000 was due to what?

It is easy for my hon. friend to take credit to himself and to his party and say that they were saving the people taxation in those days. They were adding and did add $92,000,000 of taxation that had to be met at some time and had to be met rather quickly if this country was not to go into bankruptcy. What about the following year? In 1921-22 the revenues amounted to $382,000,000 and the expenditures to $463,000,000, or another addition to the debt of this country of $81,000,000, not on war account, but on account of the ordinary business of government. Then we came into office and we were confronted, as I have said, with the obligations which hon. gentlemen opposite left to us. Our first effort was to readjust finances so as to bring about a balancing of expenditures and revenues. In the first year it was impossible completely to avoid a further deficit; but let me give the house the figures for that year. The first criticism was that we should include in the general expenditures cf the government expenditures made on account of the Canadian National Railways, and hon. gentlemen have repeated that over and over again. With respect to expenditures on the Canadian National Railways, may I [DOT]say that there is no reason why those expenditures should be included in the public accounts as part of the ordinary expenditures of the government, and this for the following reasons: First, they never have been; from . the days of confederation down to the present time the railway accounts have been kept separate. In the second place, the Canadian National Railways is in the nature of an industrial enterprise which is being operated not at cost but for purposes of profit and gain. It is in competition with a great private enterprise, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and if a just policy is to be exercised towards all the railways in this country, we must permit the Canadian National Railways to seek to make '.heir profits just as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company seek to make theirs. In the third place the whole control of the government railways has been taken out of the hands of the administration; the railways have been placed under the control of a president and board of directors who, by authority of parliament, are completely-removed from any control on the part of the administration. I ask whether in those circumstances it would be fair and proper that the accounts of the Canadian National railways should be made part of the ordinary government expenditures.
But more than that. As has been very properly said in this debate, the Canadian National Railways are on all fours with a large industrial enterprise, such as the Hydro-Electric m the province of Ontario-an industrial enterprise which is in the nature of a great business corporation giving service to the public at large, but being conducted along

lines similar to those followed by any large industrial enterprise. Every industrial corporation looking to the future will make outlays in the present with the expectation that returns will come in the course of a period of years. That has been the case with the Canadian National Railways. When one looks at the advances that have been made to the Canadian National Railways, one will discover that while money has been advanced from parliament to the Canadian National Railways, it has gone into improvements of a character which, though it may take years to bring results, we nevertheless expect in the course of time, will more and more justify the advances which have been made. May I point out this difference between the advances made by hon. gentlemen opposite to the Canadian National Railways and the advances made by the present administration? For the most part the advances which hon. gentlemen opposite made went to meet deficits in operation. The advances which have been made by the present administration have for the most part gone into improvements and extensions of a character likely vastly to increase the revenues of the railway in the course of time.

The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), speaking in this house the other day, said that it was a new idea to have an outside auditor come in and audit the books of the government, but my hon. friend from West York agrees that when he was in office as Finance Minister he engaged this firm of chartered accountants to audit the boks. When the
house rose at six o'clock I was about to take up the representations of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) with respect to the public debt of the Dominion. I notice that in his presentation this afternoon my hon. friend took an attitude somewhat different from that which he assumed when speaking on the address. On that occasion he intimated that the government had increased the public debt. He alleged that the government was responsible for the increase of the debt in the fiscal year 1921-22 and in the fiscal year 192223. He did not repeat that comparison this afternoon, but I should like nevertheless to point out to him at this juncture how unfair it was. The fiscal year 1921-22 was the year in which his friends were in office during nine months out of the twelve. The present administration came into office in December 1921, and, as I said this afternoon, the budget of that year had been prepared by a Minister of Finance who was a member of the Conservative government of the time. Therefore the responsibility for the relation of the revenues to expenditures was entirely attributable to the budget as then brought down; and that budget occasioned an increase in the public debt of $81,000,000. It is not argument but a species of legerdemain to charge this government with that increase in the debt; it must be ascribed to hon. gentlemen opposite. And the increase in the following year, the increase of some $31,000,000 odd1, was inevitable in view of the large amount of obligations which were left on the doorstep of the present administration, which had to be met before we could begin to deal in any adequate measure with the necessities of the public service. The correct comparison, as I have already stated, is between the two years for the most part of office of hon. gentlemen apposite prior to the time at which the present government took office, the years 1920-21, and 1921-22 and the three years succeeding, which was a period of financial readjustment leading to surpluses instead of deficits, as well as the three years following that, of which this is the third, and which is a period of tax and debt reduction.

For the two years ending 1921 and 1922 the addition to the debt was $92,000,000 in the one case and $81,000,000 in the other, or a total additional debt in those two years of $173,000,000. Now in the first three years of Liberal administration, which I have called the period of financial readjustment, the increase in the debt, taking the year ending 1923, was $62,000,000; in the following year there was not an increase but a reduction in the debt to the extent of $36,000,000; while in the subsequent year there was a reduction of some $300,000 odd. In other words, it took three years for the present administration to get the affairs of the country so readjusted as to have surpluses replace the deficits of the old administration. From that time on we have had continuously surpluses as follows: In the year ending 1926, $28,000,000; 1927, $42,000,000; and this year we have a surplus of $38,000,000-a surplus which would have amounted to $54,000,000 had the Minister of Finance not written off the bad debts which grew out of loans made by our predecessors for soldier land settlement and for relief in the form of seed grain.
Not only has the present administration reduced the public debt in the manner I have indicated, but we have also considerably reduced the burden which the taxpayers of the country must carry, in meeting interest on the debt, by the system of refunding at a lower rate of interest which the present Minister of Finance has brought about. The present minister found that hon. gentlemen opposite had been making loans at high rates of interest over long periods and he immediately set to work to see whether it was not possible, by refunding, to reduce these loans and to issue new loans at lower rates of

Now I come to the next subject dealt with by my hon. friend opposite. Throughout this debate an effort has been made on the part of the opposition to have it appear that the reductions in taxation which we have been steadily making are in the last analysis simply the equivalent of the additional taxation which, after we came into office, we found it necessary to impose. As I have already pointed out to hon. gentlemen opposite this additional taxation was necessary to meet their debts; it was necessary to meet the obligations which they had left to us. I take issue with my hon. friends opposite in the allegation that the reduction of taxation which we have effected is merely the corresponding equivalent of the increase. What were the taxes which we found imposed when we came into office? There were, of course, the duties of customs and excise, but there were also the special war taxes such as the income tax, the sales tax and the tax upon cheques, promissory notes and the like. In the year ending 1922 we added a tax on receipts, we slightly increased the tax on cheques and on promissory notes and bills of exchange, and made some changes in the sales tax. But these taxes we have long since reduced to a point lower than they were at the time we came' into office.
The sales tax was a tax which as I have said we did increase slightly, but we did away with

the system of pyramiding which under hon. gentlemen opposite had existed, and which made the sales tax very much higher in reality than it has ever been since 1923. We have exempted from the operation of the sales tax an increasing number of articles; we have cut the tax in half in some cases, and once we had discharged the special obligations which it was increased to meet, we have steadily reduced its rate.
With respect to the income tax, again the record of this government has been one of reduction, but not reduction of taxation with increase of debt; it has been reduction of taxation accompanied by reduction of the public debt. I wish to stress that point to hon. members of the house, because I would agree with those who say that there is no justification for reducing the income tax so long as we are adding to the general debt of the country, and so long as the public debt of the country is not being paid off at an appreciable rate. I would point out to hon. members, however, that this year for example we have paid off of the public debt, taking the bad loans to which I have referred, the sum of $54,000,000, which is very much iu advance of the sum suggested by the leader of the opposition this afternoon as an annual reduction in the public debt under the scheme which he thought should be adopted as a

That tax does not exist today ; it was abolished in 1926; in that regard it cannot be said that we are now taking off a tax which we imposed. Then consider the tax on cheques, bills of exchange, promissory notes and other documents. When we came into office we found a tax of two cents on every cheque, bill of exchange and promissory note, and in our first year in office we provided that there should be a tax of two cents on every additional $50, with a maximum tax of $2, which was reduced to $1 in 1923. The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
Now may I say just a word with regard to the clause in the amendment which suggests that the sales tax should be entirely removed. There are two or three outstanding reasons why that is impossible or at all events inadvisable. This afternoon I gave one reason which of course is self evident; that reason was that there are heavy obligations which came down to us from the period of the war, which must be met. Taxes have to be raised somewhere and somehow and the sales tax having been in existence for some time it is perhaps advisable, if it is to be removed, that it should be removed by degrees *ather than all at once. The reason why the sales tax should be removed by degrees will be apparent to hon. members Who were in the house at the time parliament was asked to vote a large sum of money in order to make a refund to automobile dealers who had stocks of automobiles on hand when the tax on automobiles was abolished. They had paid the tax, and it was held that it was most unfair, when subsequently they were unable to pass it on to the consumers because of the reduced prices owing to the sudden change in taxation, that they should not be recompensed, and parliament decided to give them back these sums in order to reimburse them for the money which had been exacted in the form of taxation. Now in a number of instances where taxes are being reduced the practice has been followed of reducing by stages. By making the reduction at the rate of one per cent at a time the merchants and dealers are able to absorb it. If however, you take the tax off completely, you are liable to create a serious injustice to a large number of persofls in the country who have on hand supplies of the articles on which the sales tax is imposed. You are unfair towards a large class of citizens, and apt to create an uncertainty or unrest in
business which, in the net result, is bound to be baneful. So I say that if my hon. friends who have in their amendment suggested that the sales tax should be completely removed, will reconsider the matter from the point of view of what is sound business in the commercial community, they will see that the reason I have just advanced is not only a thoroughly good and effective one, but one which has been endorsed by the action of this very parliament in dealing with a situation created heretofore owing in a particular instance to the complete abolition of the tax. So much then, for the sales tax.	_
Now I come to the income tax. Here again may I stress the point that the present government, in connection with this tax as with all others, has sought to bring such relief as it could to the taxpayers of the country. One form of that relief has been in exemptions from income tax. 'I venture to say that those who are asking us to retain the tax would not ask us to restore it with respect to any of the exemptions which have been granted under it. But if the income tax is so exceptional in its character that it should be retained at all costs, it seems to me that it does not require one to go very much further to say that there should be no exemptions whatever, or that the exemptions should be exceedingly small. However, this government has sought steadily to exempt from the income tax those persons in the community who are least able to bear it. I venture to say that hon. members will be surprised, as they hear in the order of sequence in which the exemptions have taken place, how considerable they have become as the result of steady reductions year after year. When hon. gentlemen were in office the exemptions were as follows: married persons were exempted to the extent of $2,000 of their income. In the case of unmarried persons the exemption was $1,000. The allowance for each dependent child under eighteen years of age was fixed at $200. In 1922, the first year that we were in office, we increased the exemption for each child from $200 to $300. May I give to the house quite frankly the reason that actuated the government in reducing the income tax to the extent that this has been done in the present year? As hon. members know, we had in the fall of the year a conference between the provinces and the Dominion where questions of concern to the provinces were discussed very freely with the several members of the government. One question discussed was that of taxation and more particularly the delimitation of the fields of taxation. Representatives of the provinces pointed out that, while the Dominion was entitled under the constitution to raise taxes by indirect methods, such as, the customs and excise, and also by direct methods, the provinces on the other hand were restricted to direct taxation, and1 being restricted to this field they were finding it more and more difficult to raise the revenues required for the increasing services which they were being called upon to perform. The point was stressed by the provinces that in recent years many obligations have devolved upon them which require a degree of expenditure which they did not believe was wholly contemplated at confederation. There were, for instance, large expenses in connection with social legislation of one kind or another, expenses in connection with road making, expenses in regard to several other matters such as technical education, all of which are under provincial jurisdiction They further directed our attention to the circumstance that in seeking for new sources of revenue they had imposed certain taxes which had been questioned in the courts; that they had been precluded from continuing one tax after another because of some decision which had been given which made it impossible for them to enter a particular field. So the plea was made to the Dominion that we should if possible leave to the provinces certain fields of taxation, and the field of taxation that was especially mentioned in this connection was the income tax. May I direct the attention of the house to this fact? Many hon. members pay income taxes not only to the Dominion treasury but also to the provincial treasury. Some provinces of this Dominion have income taxes as a source of their revenue. British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island impose an income tax as provinces, but in addition to that, throughout the Dominion there are municipalities which also are imposing an income tax for purposes of revenue. Municipalities in Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan and possibly one other province are doing this. In some seven provinces out of

nine, income taxes are being imposed either by municipalities in those provinces or by the provinces themselves, in addition to the tax imposed by the Dominion. I confess that members of the government felt that there was much to be said for the point of view presented by the provinces that they should be permitted more latitude in regard to income taxation. Let me distinguish at once between income tax derived from the income of individuals and income tax derived from incomes of corporations. I think that incomes of corporations must always be collected by the federal government, for the reason that otherwise one or two provinces, to be concrete Ontario and Quebec, would profit at the expense of other provinces from which much of the income of these corporations is derived. It is for the most part true that in a few centres large business corporations have their headquarters. The great railway companies, insurance companies, trust companies, banks and the like have their headquarters in some of these larger cities of the Dominion and principally in the cities of Montreal and Toronto but the revenues of the corporations are drawn from all parts of the Dominion.

There is no province that has not at least a few fairly wealthy men who derive their incomes from corporations, and which very corporations have their headquarters in the provinces which I have mentioned. The point I wish to make clear is this, that as regards income tax derived from corporations, the federal government was not prepared to consider for a minute parting with that tax to the provinces. We maintain that this is a tax which ought to be and which will toe retained by the federal treasury so long, at least, as the present government has office. As I have said the government was to some extent impressed by the plea made to it by the premiers of some of the provinces in regard to the tax on the income of individuals. I remember the Premier of Manitoba suggested that not only should we give to Manitoba the tax which comes from the income of individuals but that we should collect it as well and hand over to the province the

The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glenn), who spoke the other evening, made much the same suggestion, that the income tax should be collected by the federal treasury and distributed in part to the provinces. That is a matter, in one sense, of book-keeping; but the point I wish to stress at the moment is this, that if we were to do that very thing, we would not be doing anything different in principle from what we are doing undeT the present reduction, in reducing the tax on incomes of individuals with a view to allowing the provinces that much more of freedom in the matter of their collection of taxation from individual incomes.

From the point of view of the provinces it would appear to be a question as to whether they shall be permitted to have certain fields in which they can raise the revenue (necessary, or whether they shall do as was done at the Dominion-provincial conference-complain that their field is so restricted that they cannot get the revenue necessary, and then appeal to the Dominion government to give them in subsidies what they cannot get by means of taxation.

I think we had better hold on to what we have in any form of taxation until we reach our final reckoning with the provinces.
That is all I wish to say in regard to the taxation of incomes, beyond making this clear: that not only was the government moved in this matter by the representations made by the provinces, but we were interested in ascertaining how this House of Commons would view leaving that field of taxation to the provinces. I may say that if we ever entertained an idea of giving up the individual income tax to the provinces or for any other purpose, certainly the discussion that has taken place in the house during this debate will preclude anything of the kind for the future. Hon. members need not be concerned about any policy which may be said to aim at doing away with the revenue derived from income tax.
I want to make this clear to my hon. friends, so that there will be no misunderstanding when they come to consider again their attitude towards the government on the budget.

I will give in a few moments what we did in respect to cottons and woollens a few years ago. This ought to be taken into account in connection with what is being done this year* Before I do that however, I should like to come at once to the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in regard to the tariff. May I draw attention to a circumstance which is enlightening when one reflects upon it?
The amendment proposed by hon. gentlemen opposite is on all fours with all amendments which have come from hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to matters of fiscal policy. Notwithstanding what they have said in their speeches on public platforms and what we know to be implied in their utterances in

parliament and in the amendments as drawn, they have always carefully avoided ever dividing this house on the subject of protection. At every general election the country is told by my hon. friends of the opposition that what is needed for Canadian industry is more protection. This appeal is made because it is effective as directed to individual localities, one at a time. It is possible, for example, for Conservative candidates to appeal for protection in British Columbia with respect to certain classes of industry, such as fruit-growing, lumbering and the like, then in another province, Ontario, to appeal for protection for the large factories that are scattered up and down this province; and in the maritime provinces to make their appeal for protection to suit certain localities there; but when it comes to taking a consensus of view of the Dominion as a whole, as it expresses itself in this House of Commons, hon. gentlemen run away every time and evade the direct issue-they fail to bring in an amendment advocating protection.
Take the general election of 1921. From one end of the Dominion to the other our Conservative friends informed the electors that what was needed to save the country was more protection, that this alone would prevent men from emigrating to the United States, that this alone would prevent unemployment, that this alone would revive industry. But when the hon. gentlemen came back to this house in 1922 and had an opportunity of moving their first amendment, was it an amendment for increased protection? No, their amendment completely avoided any such profession of faith on their part. It was much like the amendment before the house to-day-an amendment of regrets; it regretted that up to that time the resolutions of the Liberal convention of 1919 had not been carried out in full. In the session of 1923 they failed to bring in any amendment whatsoever. In the session of 1924 they waited until my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) brought in an amendment on the cost of living; then they became very courageous and, knowing that the rules at that time only permitted one amendment, they moved an amendment in favour of a protective policy consistently maintained, and of course it was ruled out of order. Next we come to the session of 1925, just before the general election, and my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) presented an amendment regretting that there had not been more done in the way of tax reduction. Then in
1925	we had another general election and throughout the country the doctrine of protection was again preached by hon. gentlemen opposite, but when they came back to this house in 1926 did they move any amendment along the line of protection? They did bring in an amendment, but what was it? We had undertaken to reduce the duty on automobiles. Their amendment was not in regard to their policy of protection at all, but was directed purely and simply to the procedure which we had followed. They said we had laid down a policy when we appointed the tariff board of investigation before tariff change, and they complained that before introducing in this house any revision of the tariff on automobiles we should have secured the opinion of the tariff board. To-day when we come to the house with a tariff revision based upon investigations made by the tariff board, our friends of the opposition complain of our ever having approached the board. In
1926	was another election and more talk of the need for protection. After the election of 1926, having talked so much of protection throughout the campaign, did they bring in an amendment advocating their fiscal policy? Not at all; they let the session go by without moving an amendment. This year they move an amendment in the old form, an amendment which is full of regrets but does not contain a single statement of the fiscal policy on which they are supposed to be united, and not a word of their real convictions. No, it is simply the sort of thing one sees at hallowe'en, when little boys appear on the streets in false faces. Our Conservative friends come here with an amendment which is nothing other than a false face, something very fair to look upon-just as the words of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition this afternoon were fair to listen to-but back of it all if you take away the false face, as hon. members well know, you get the ugly mien of protection for special interests, which have always been the particular care of hon. gentlemen opposite.

I gather that his chief objection to the tariff board is that the chairman, Mr. Moore, was a candidate at the last general election and therefore should not have been appointed to such a position. At the time to which I have reference he was neither a candidate nor a prospective candidate but actually a member of parliament. Moreover, he was Minister of Finance. And he went from one end of the country to the other, taking evidence, doing the very thing Mr. Moore is doing to-day. No one took exception to that; no one attacked it on the ground that the method was wrong, for as a matter of fact that was the method which had been generally practised in connection with revisions of the tariff until the present advisory board on tariff and taxation was appointed. Until then ministers of the crown travelled from one end of the country to the other

summoning interested persons from whatever quarter they might wish to come to appear before them to give evidence. That evidence was sifted and the ministers brought down such recommendations as they deemed advisable in the way of tariff revision. It was found, however, that this method was not as satisfactory as having a detailed investigation made by experts week by week, month by month and year by year-an investigation such as the present tariff board is able to make. Let me point out to hon. gentlemen, however, that the tariff advisory board does not in the exercise of its functions in any way take away from the power of the government and of parliament in dealing with the tariff itself. and quoting from the sources which they have quoted against us, there were no less than 742,000 Canadians who left Canada for the United States, according to the immigration figures in that ten-year period, yet the census which keeps a record of those who actually settled and remained in the country shows that there were 70,000 fewer Canadians in the United States in 1920 than there were in 1910. As a matter of fact, as everyone knows, immigration has been going on back and forth across the frontier ever since the beginnings of the two countries. Lord Durham in his report in 1839 refers to the emigration from Canada to the United States at that time and deplores it, and so you find it all along. But the statistics at present go to show conclusively that the numbers leaving this country are fewer and fewer, and on the other hand that the total number of immigrants entering Canada from other countries has been increasing year by year during the last few years.
I should like to have said a few words in regard to the question of trade, but I Shall pass over that with a single reference to our trajde with Australia and New Zealand. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in speaking this afternoon about our trade with Australia and New Zealand, said that every treaty we had made had been against the interests of Canada. What are the facts?
The facts regarding the trade between Australia and Canada-and I would like my hon. friend to remember this in his advocacy of empire trade-are that on an average over a period of years for every dollar's worth of goods we have bought and buy from Australia and New Zealand they have bought and buy three dollars' worth from us. In addition, the goods that we have been sending to Australia and New Zealand have been for the most part the very class of goods which hon. gentlemen opposite, in accordance with their theories, say that we should export, namely, manufactured goods. Our exports for the most part have been automobiles, implements, rubber, paper, lumber, canned fish, and other classes of products which are manufactured. I think something like ninety per cent of the commodities we have sold to Australia and New Zealand have been raw materials manufactured into the finished articles in this country. The port of Vancouver has grown to be one of the great ports of the world, and if that port is going to continue to grow, it will be through the growth of our Pacific trade, yet hon. gentlemen opposite, when we have a trade with another part of the empire in the proportion 56103-831
of three to one in favour of this country, say that we ought to cease that trade, notwithstanding that it is the very class of trade they are advocating, namely the export of manufactured products. So I say hon. gentlemen opposite are again wrong in their contention that the policies of this government are not meeting the situation.
My hon. friend has been making a great many speeches in various parts of the Dominion, in all of which he has stressed the point that our development in trade means "parting with our estate"-our natural resources. He says we are selling our estate. Well, let us get first of all a true perspective of what constitutes the estate of Canada. Take agriculture. What is the position of this portion of Canada's estate? It is estimated that the total arable land of Canada amounts to three hundred million acres. Now, not more than a fifth of that total is under cultivation at the present time. Can it be said that when we grow wheat and sell it from the land under cultivation we are parting with our agricultural estate? We send the raw products abroad in order to get money back wherewith to create a demand for our manufactures and other commodities. That is the position in regard to agriculture.
Now let me take timber. The estimated total forest area of Canada is in the neighbourhood of 1,200,000 square miles. Forty per cent of this is covered with merchantable timber. There is not another timber area of equal extent in the world outside Siberia. As a matter of fact, we have not begun to appreciate even the extent of these resources. But is not the preservation of this part of our estate very largely a question of conservation, and are not a large proportion of our timber resources under the control of the provincial governments? It is to those governments that my hon. friend should address his remarks

rather than to the federal government. We are co-operating with the provinces in conserving the forests. Much more harm is done to our forests through loss by insects and fire than by lumbering operations. Some of the provinces have a statutory requirement that before the timber is exported it must to a certain degree be manufactured. Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and one or two of the other provinces have enacted such regulations. It can be shown that a very large quantity of our forest wealth is leaving Canada to-day only in the form of the manufactured product.
Another part of our estate is our minerals. Is there any hon. member who will attempt even to estimate the extent of the mineral wealth of Canada? How can it be said that we are parting with that estate when we sell some raw material from a portion of the earth that has been little more than scratched? Every year we are discovering new areas of mineral wealth, and what there may be ultimately available in the way of production no one can yet foresee.
Another portion of our estate is represented by our fisheries-ocean, river and lake. So far as our ocean fisheries are concerned we know nothing of depletion; as to the fisheries of our lakes and rivers, the governments of the provinces and the Dominion authorities are co-operating by means of hatcheries and in other ways to conserve and increase this important natural resource. So there again any reference to losing our estate seems to me to be wide of the mark.
Then take our water-powers; a few years ago we did not even regard them as an asset; to-day they are one of our greatest assets. This government has laid down the policy that the export of hydro-electric power shall be prohibited so that these great reserves of energy may be utilized in building up the Dominion. We have available forty-one million horse-power, of which at present only four and three-quarter million has been developed.
But in speaking of our natural resources, emphasis must be laid upon the word "resource" as well as upon the word "natural". A resource is something to be used in case of need, when it is required. That is what these resources were given to us for by nature-not to be left dormant, but to be used. The extent to which they can be used and what they will produce depends upon the application of science and human energy. Science is continually finding new means of developing our natural resources.
