few years ago were regarded as worthless; to-day, through scientific processes, those ores are becoming increasingly valuable. So in regard to wheat and grain, frost-resisting qualities have been discovered iu the course of evolving new varieties, and the effect will be to roll back the map of this Dominion further and further north. And yet hon. gentlemen opposite say that we are not to export any of these raw materials, that they must be made into manufactured goods to supply the home market. May 1 draw their attention to this fact?-We could not more effectively destroy the home market than by following their suggestion. If we put aside the proportion of wheat that is exported, we find that we are importing more in the way of raw materials than we are exporting. Do hon. gentlemen mean to say that we can lay down to the world the doctrine that we will not export any of our raw materials, and at the same time expect other nations to supply us with their raw materials for our cotton mills, our woollen mills and our rubber factories? If we want to trade with the world we have to be prepared to sell them what they are prepared to buy from us. If you take the total of our exports-I will not trouble the house to go through the list, but any hon. member can look up the year book-you will find that for the most part the various commodities are as far advanced in the manufactured state as they can be. Not all of them, it is true. For instance, wheat might be manufactured into flour. What would be the effect if we were to follow the doctrine of hon. gentlemen opposite? If we refused to sell our wheat unless manufactured into flour, the nations that to-day are buying our wheat would turn to some other countries for their supply and we would lose our market altogether. The reason that wheat is exported rather than flour is that it can be handled in bulk cargo, whereas flour is handled in package cargo. Besides, the countries that import wheat do not want it in the form of flour. More than that, the great flour-milling industries in the United States grind our wheat in bond, exporting the flour and retaining the by-products. Under the circumstances, it is doubtful whether any effective action could be taken which would secure the grinding of our wheat for our own flour mills. It is far more likely any such action would jeopardize our exports of wheat which must be sold in competition with the wheat of other countries on the markets of the importing nations. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the more one considers the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite the more untenable it appears to be.
I will conclude with a brief reference to one or two matters of a different nature which have been referred to in this debate. The first was a reference by my hon. friend from Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards), to what transpired in a previous session of parliament. He mentioned that, shortly before it left office in 1926, on three occasions the Liberal administration was defeated. May I read his statement:
It is likewise true that on June 25, 1926, the King government was defeated three times in one day.
* My only reason for raising this question at the moment is that in my opinion it is just as well to be accurate in any matter touching the records of parliament. Let me say that the government which I had the honour to lead prior to my resignation in June, 1926, was never once defeated. Had the government been defeated the fact would appear in the records of parliament. I have in my hand the votes and proceedings of the 25th day of June, containing t'he proceedings of parliament on that date. What were the various resolutions submitted to the judgment of the house on that occasion? There was one resolution moved by the 'hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), defeated by a vote of 115 to 117. That motion was defeated. Will anyone say that the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was a government motion, and that because that resolution failed to receive the support of t'he house the government was thereby defeated? Then there was an appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, to which exception was taken by the leader of t'he opposition. Appeal was taken by the then leader of the opposition from your ruling to the house, the house being asked whether the ruling of the Chair should be sustained. The house on a vote of 117 to 115 failed to sustain that ruling, but that, Mr. Speaker, I regard as a reflection upon the opposition and its leader rather than upon either the government or the Chair. And what was the next motion? The next motion was one moved by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) and seconded by the late Mr. King of North Huron, a member of t'he Progressive party, "that the debate be now adjourned". By a majority of one that motion was defeated; the vote was 114 to 115. Will anyone contend that that was a government motion and that in consequence of its failure to carry the government was defeated? There was one further motion, it was moved by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lavigueur). It was the only motion which
1296	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
came from this side of the house, it was "that the debate be now adjourned". The record in the votes and proceedings of that day shows this motion as having been agreed to; and this was the last motion put in that parliament, for it was a day or two following that I tendered my resignation to His Excellency the Governor General. The house adjourned on Friday and being denied a dissolution, I tendered my resignation before the house reassembled on Monday. It is, I say, just as well that the public be correctly informed in respect of the records on this question.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask
a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the government, of which my right hon. friend has the honour to be the head, ever been sustained by the popular vote of the country since 1921?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In answer to
my hon. friend I will say that the government of which I have been the head since 1921 assumed office by virtue of the will of the people of this country, and has retained office in virtue of the support it has received from this House of Commons. The government, let me add, is in office to-dav by reason of the votes of the people of Canada and in virtue of the confidence reposed in it by the House of Commons. But let me remind my hon. friend that there was another so-called government formed in the short interval between my resignation and the time the government resumed power. Of that short-lived phantom administration my hon. friend was not a member, and I imagine he is proud of the fact; no doubt he is happy to have been left out of it. However, there is one fact to be observed in relation to that government, and that is, that it never had the confidence either of the House of Commons or of the country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I say-

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sit down.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It had the confidence of the people to the extent of over 100.000 votes more than my hon. friend's government received.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, all I can say to my hon. friend is, there is a perfectly obvious answer to his remarks and it is that we are over here and he is over there.
Now, speaking of the confidence of the electorate in governments, my hon. friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), adfMr. Mackenzie King.]
dressing the house the other evening on the budget, touched upon one or two matters which I consider subjects of reasonable and proper debate; I refer particularly to what she had to say in regard to the constitution of parliament and to certain matters of procedure in the House of Commons. One question she brought up was the right of dissolution, and this comes up in connection, with what I have just been, saying. My hon. friend expressed the view that the power of dissolution should not rest with the Prime Minister but that-if I understand her correctly-there should be a fixed parliamentary term. It seems to me that many of these matters of form appear differently when we come to the reality. When one comes to examine the so-called right of the prime minister to request dissolution it is obvious that no one individual has the power at his will and caprice, to dissolve parliament at any particular moment. The fact is that the Prime Minister gives expression to the view of his cabinet, and the cabinet gives expression to the view of what it considers to be the will of the majority in parliament at the time that decision is reached which leads the Prime Minister to ask for a dissolution. So that the expression of opinion of the Prime Minister, in asking for dissolution, is the expression not of an individual but of parliament as constituted at the time. I would direct the attention of the house to this important fact. Comparisons are frequently made between our system of government and the system in the United States where there is a fixed legislative term. When these comparisons are made this essential fact seems to be ignored: Where there is a fixed term of office, a period of four years as in the United States, the executive is completely independent of the legislature. The executive in the United States, the president and his cabinet, take office under oath to devote their whole time to the administration of government. They have nothing to do with legislation; they are not responsible to the legislature.	They are
bound only by their oath of office and are assured of office for the period of time designated under the constitution. The British system is entirely different. Under the British system ministers of the crown have not only responsible executive duties to perform; they must come into parliament, as the ministers of the government of this Dominion do, and assume the responsibility for such legislation as is enacted. They must take the responsibility for the administration of the affairs of the country as well as for the proceedings of parliament. Under the latter svs-

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
tem of government you have a condition which makes it imperative, in circumstances in which the executive finds, it impossible, being manacled or thwarted, to continue the conduct of public business, that the administration, through the Prime Minister, should have the right to appeal to the judgment of the people. I know that my hon. friend from Southeast Grey feels equally strongly with myself on the rights of the people. After all where is the wrong in giving to the Prime Minister the right to ask for a dissolution of parliament? Is dissolution not an appeal from a comparatively few members of the House of Commons to the great body of public opinion? After all, is it not based on trust in the people? When the Prime Minister asks for a dissolution of parliament, what is it for which he appeals? He simply asks for the right to allow the people themselves to judge in relation to the conduct of those whom they have made theft trustees. I hold, therefore, that no finer doctrine of the rights of the people could be propounded than that which ensures, in times of crisis, or when any measure comes up of paramount importance to the public welfare on which the people have not been consulted, that the people shall be given the right to pronounce upon the question. In other words, the Prime Minister asks for the right to go to the people, from whom all power is derived, in order to ascertain whether or not he and his colleagues are right in the particular course which they are pursuing or intend to pursue. That point I wish to make clear because I think there are many instances in which, under the British constitution, the reality is so profoundly different from the appearance of things and that we cannot examine too deeply into what is fundamental in questions of this nature. Our system of government, which has grown up-not over a period of decades, not over a period of twenty or fifty or a hundred years, but through centuries of time-has, I believe, reached the point where it cannot be surpassed by anj' other form of government to be found anywhere else in the world.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister mean to imply that the British form of government, as we know it and as we have seen it exemplified in Canada, has reached perfection and that it cannot be improved?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I believe that so long as we are human there will always be room for improvement. I do say, however, that the British system has developed t.o a greater point of improvement and more
nearly approximates perfection than any other political system in the world. Let me assure the house that in this regard I am speaking as a minister of the crown who, being responsible for legislation which parliament is asked to consider, feels very keenly the force of what he is saying on this question.
Similarly I believe that under the British system, as demonstrated over a very long period, the most effective way of making principles and policies prevail in legislation, is by great parties composed of individuals who have in common certain principles which they desire to advocate and support. The other evening my hon. friend spoke about the feeling which is held by herself and a number of those surrounding her, that they are in parliament for the purpose of representing a class. I think I am right in placing that construction on her words; if I am wrong I hope she will correct me. May I ask her first of all one question: If we each of us took that view what would become of government in an orderly fashion?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We would have honest government; everyone would know whom we represented here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That, I submit, is a matter of opinion. However, I may say to my hon. friend that before you can even take that position in parliament you must get into parliament, and the results over a number of years have demonstrated that the only really effective way for any body of opinion to find expression in legislation through debate on the floor of parliament ig to have a party large enough and strong enough to elect enough members to give expression to that opinion in parliament itself.
In speaking the other evening my hon. friend used these words:
.	.	.	. agriculture said: This kind of thing
is no good; we are going to organize ourselves as an industry. They said to themselves: Our politics is our business, and we have been foolish in letting other people look after our business: we will never do well that way; We will send people to Ottawa, we will choose them, finance and elect them; we will control them.
Notice those words:
. . . . we will send people to Ottawa; wre will choose them, finance and elect them; we will control them.
My hon. friend remembers what took place in North Huron, where there was a member of her group who took exactly this view and who was running as a candidate in a recent by-election. I have in my hand the manifesto which he irsued during that campaign, which is in words very much like the words my
129S	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
hon. friend uttered. It is signed by Sheldon Bricker the Progressive candidate, and he uses these words in his election manifesto:
Surely agriculture, our basic industry, needs representation in the Dominion house, unfettered by party ties; free to vote on the merits of each question as it arises.
That statement was issued by the Progressive candidate in that election. Now let me return to what my hon. friend said:
.. .we will send people to Ottawa; we will choose them, finance and elect them;
Is Mr. Bricker here as a member of the Progressive group, sitting where the late Mr. King sat in this house? What was the result of having chosen a representative of a class group as a candidate? The result is that you have sitting in the Tory group opposite a gentleman who is going to cast a vote against the Progressives, against the Liberals and not at all in accord with the principles that my hon. friend has laid down as those which she supports. The point I wish to bring out is that parties are not as some suppose wrong in themselves. They are a means to an end.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Does not the Prime Minister think every party represents a distinct class?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I do not agree at all with that view; that is exactly where I differ from my hon. friend. I say that as far as the Liberal party is concerned its members represent the people as a whole, and no particular class. In the ranks of our party we have men who come from farming communities and others who come from the business world; we also have those whose lives have been given up to learned professions, but they are all united not by a class tie or bond which separates them from those belonging to the other classes in this house but by a tie which binds them in the advocacy of certain principles and policies which they hope to make prevail in legislation. It is quite true that no one can have his own way; no. one can go the full length he might wifh to go, but the advantage of a party is that it brings together men and women with like sympathies, like aims and like purposes in the advocacy of measures that they believe to be in the public interest. That is why I am touching on the question at the moment. I feel a great sympathy with many of the objects which my hon. friends of the Progressive group pursue; I would like to see some of the measures in which they are interested enacted as legislation, but I say honestly and frankly from my experience in matters of government that the fact that they hold

themselves aloof and do not avowedly co-operate with other groups in this house makes it so much more difficult to get action on some of these matters than would otherwise be the case.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the Prime Minister mean to say that this group have not cooperated with his government every time the government brought down legislation in which
we were interested?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want my hon. friend to misunderstand me; if she will look at my words she will see that I spoke comparatively. It makes it more difficult to do many things that otherwise night be done. Let me be concrete: There are a number of members in the Progressive group opposite who come from the province of Alberta. Time and again I have heard the Minister of the Interior urge that certain matters be pressed forward concerning that province, and I have seen him do his utmost to bring about progress in particular measures, but before he can get this House of Commons to support his views he has to have the support of others who have been made to think and feel as he does. Now let me ask this: Does my hon. friend think my task as leader of the government or the task of the Minister of the Interior with respect to Alberta is made any easier by the fact that most of the members from Alberta are sitting in the opposite corner and not one of them where he can most effectively use his persuasive powers with other members on this side of the house?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So I struck
home again.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister really want me to answer that question? I think it is very much easier for him and for the Minister of the Interior to bring down legislation in the interests of Alberta, because the Alberta men are outside the government and are therefore in a position to use their individuality and their brains to induce the government to bring in the legislation,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, in that
my hon. friend is mistaken. May I direct this argument to her in connection with what I am now saying: She personally has found that in order to get those sitting around her to see her viewpoint it is advisable to have discussed together many matters of policy within a little group which is termed a caucus. What is necessary with the few opposite is equally necessary if agreement is to be reached by the larger numbers here assembled. What

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
I wish to say is that all government is in the last analysis, a matter of opinion. That opinion is most generally the result of persuasion, not of coercion. In the long run more of service can be done to any particular cause or any particular locality by the sharing with others of responsibility in the fullest possible way in the support of a particular cause or what may be desired for a particular locality. That is my reason and my sole reason for preferring the party system to what my hon. friend refers to as representation by class.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do the Liberal-Progressives attend the Liberal caucuses?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will say a
word to my hon. friend with regard to the Liberal-Progressives. They are pretty closely in touch with opinion on this side of the house, and I think we on our part endeavour to give full regard to what the Liberal-Progressives have to say. To my hon. friend who interrupted me, may I point out just where the line of reasoning which he takes is apt to lead, and how serious may be the false position into which it may bring him. He made a statement in this house the other evening to the effect that the most effective way a class group could act might be to see what bargain it could make with a party whose known principles were wholly opposed to its own. What were his words? He said:
.	.	.	. the only thing for us to do is to go
and make the very best possible deal with the protectionists and see what they can do for us.
Now those are the words of my hon. friend. How are they viewed in the country? Here is the Montreal Gazette which represents the Conservative party and I think represents in the best way what is in the best interest of that party. What does it say, contrasting the point of view of the Conservative party with the point of view of my hon. friend? It says:
Whether the member for Peace River used the word "deal" or the word "bargain"- reports of his remarks differ in this respect- is not very material, the sense being the same. It is unfortunate that he did not express more clearly his idea of what the protectionist "can do for us".
Then it goes on to say:
But the Conservative party is still founded upon the principle of protection, and there can be no "deal" and no "bargain" which involves a surrender of that principle. The Conservative policy is not in the market.
That is the position which the Montreal Gazette takes.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is this budget which has been presented to the house a protectionist budget or not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like my hon. friend to wait a minute. Probably he does not wish to hear what some of the other papers are saying. Here is the Financial Times of Montreal. How does it regard my hon. friend's remarks? I shall not read the whole article, but it says in interpreting the point of view which he is now presenting:
Indeed Mr. Kennedy's offer-the way in which he puts that support up for sale-is hedged about by a most unacceptable condition.
Evidently it regards my hon. friend's attitude as one not of maintaining but of selling principles.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to dose. My only reason for quoting the remarks of my hon. friend was that he rose and thereby directed my attention to a matter which I had already covered in my notes but which I had for the moment thought of passing over. I am very glad that the hon. gentleman interrupted me for this reason: His attitude has helped to make clear that the moment you attempt to govern on the basis of class representation that moment you begin to cause just the kind of suspicion with regard to motives that is set out in articles I have quoted, namely that, the whole business is a matter of bargaining. I know my hon. friend from Southeast Grey believes in representative government, but I ask her is it possible to have representative government where members sit in parliament as the representatives of a class, and do not sit as representing all classes.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No one can represent all classes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those who advocate class government also believe, I think, in democratic government. But government by a majority is the only way in which it is possible to express the voice of democracy. Class representation may be described as an attempt at government not by a majority but by a minority. Hon. members of the Progressive group say we desire power. So do they; the difference between them and ourselves is one of method. The method under the parliamentary representation system is the method of gaining and maintaining power through persuasion and co-operation. As interpreted by my hon. friend from Peace River, the method to be employed is not so much one of cooperation as it is one of coercion.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister laid stress on the importance of numbers. May

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
I point out that when Nova Scotia had a full quota in the Liberal ranks that province had less relief by a long way than it has had since most of its members have sat on the other side of the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall deal with that point at another time. I notice, Mr.. Speaker, that I have already taken up more time than I intended. I have no desire to enter into any argument. I was simply trying to make clear to some of my hon. friends opposite with whose point of view on many things I have the utmost sympathy, how a government is situated in the matter of making policies prevail, and I do say that hon. members from Manitoba who sit here as Progressive Liberals, associating day by day with the members of the Liberal party, speaking with the different members of the party, and giving the government in an intimate way the benefit of their opinions and advice and their support, are doing much more to ensure the enactment of legislation in this parliament in accordance with the principles they have most at heart than would have been possible had they been sitting on the opposite side and away from the government altogether.
May I say this in conclusion? The leader of the Progressive group in speaking the other day on the death of Lord Oxford and Asquith said he believed' that Mr. Asquith would be remembered in history more for what he had done in the way of legislation for the benefit of the masses in the shape of old age pensions and the like, than for anything else he had accomplished. I ask my hon. friends where would Mr. Asquith's legislation on old age pensions have been if he had' gone into the
House of Commons of Great Britain as a lawyer, determined to sit there as a representative of the legal profession? I ask my hon. friends to take all the leaders in the public life of Great Britain, I ask them to take all that has been achieved in the matter of social reform legislation, and I ask them where that legislation would have come from if men of many callings and professions had not stood up and fought the battles of the people in the matter of the franchise, in the matter of the tariff, in the matter of the factory laws, the mining laws, and other legislation deeply affecting the interests of the masses. Had many of the great men whose names are household words been in parliament only as the representatives of a particular class, where should we have got the legislation which they were responsible for enacting-men like Gladstone, like Bright, like Cobden, like Huskisson, like Shaftesbury, and others of great eminence none of whom ever sat in parliament as the representatives of a particular class? They represented the people as a whole and the liberal doctrines which they professed were implemented' into legislation for the benefit of the country as a whole. We as Liberals consider with them that the duty of members of parliament is not to represent a class only or the people in only one section of the country but men and women of all classes in all parts of the country, and that to this end we should work in cooperation and close association with our fellow members of kindred sympathies and views for the greatest good to the greatest number throughout our broad Dominion.

Textile Changes under Budget of 1928 Cottons
The maximum duty under the General Tariff is reduced from 374 per cent to 30 per cent, with a single exception.
Cotton yarns, 40's and finer, are made dutiable but the rates are reduced on the coarser counts of yarn.
Gray (unbleached) cotton fabrics are reduced by 2J per cent in the intermediate and general tariffs.
Printed and dyed cottons are reduced 24 per cent in the British preference, 5 per cent in the intermediate and 5 per cent in the general tariff.
Yarn-dyed fabrics are reduced 24 per cent British preference, 5 per cent in the intermediate and 24 per cent general.
On a large range of household cottons, such as tablecloths, counterpanes, sheets, quilts, towels, plain curtains, etc., there are reductions of from 5 to 10 per cent in the British preference rate, from 24 to 5 per cent in the intermediate, and from 24 to 5 per cent in the general.
Blankets of cotton are reduced 74 per cent in the British preference rate, the intermediate and the general.
Cotton embroideries, laces, etc., are reduced, roughly, 5 per cent on all tariffs.
Cotton clothing and manufactures of cotton show reductions ranging from 24 to 5 per cent on all tariffs, (with very few exceptions, due to reclassification).
Woollens
Yarns for weaving are reduced from various duty ranges (chiefly 124, 174 and 20) to Free under the British preference rate, 10 under the intermediate and 124 under the general rate.
Dress goods in the gray for dyeing or finishing in Canada are reduced 5 per cent under the British preference rate.
Lustres and linings are reduced from 20, 30 and 35 per cent to 10, 20 and 25 per cent.
Woollen fabrics not over 5 ounces in weight per square yard are reduced 24 per cent in the British preference rate.
Cheaper ranges of woollen socks and stockings are reduced 5 per cent in all tariffs.
Knitted goods of all kinds valued at not more than 90 cents per pound are reduced 5 per cent in the British preference rate.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the house ready for the question? Before I put the question, I wish to address myself to hon. members on both sides of the house. Standing order 7, under our new rule, reads as follows:
At 11 of the clock, p.m., unless the closure rule be then in operation, the proceedings on any business under consideration shall be interrupted and Mr. Speaker shall adjourn the house without question put, provided that all business not disposed of at the termination of the sitting shall stand over until the next sitting day when it will be taken up at the same stage where its progress was interrupted.
I wish to point out that it is not yet 11 o'clock, but that hour will soon be reached, and there are three votes to be taken this evening. It is not only probable but quite certain that by 11 o'clock the three divisions will not have been taken. I should like to know, therefore, the sense of the house as to whether we shall proceed with the three votes notwithstanding the hour. Am I to understand that such is the unanimous wish of the house?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker; I cannot agree, if any question be not put at 11 o'clock, to giving my consent to the breaking of the rule. I consider that these rules are binding, and that we must suffer the consequences of our absurdity.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a collective "absurdity" voted by the house last year.

If the house is to proceed, consent must be unanimous. Bourinot says:
Each house is bound by every consideration of self-interest and justice to observe strictly its rules and standing orders, and to rebuke every attempt to evade or infringe them. Consequently the Senate and House of Commons never permit their rules and standing orders to be suspended, unless by unanimous consent.
Does the hon. gentleman persist in his opposition?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order I would like to point out to you that last year a similar situation arose when an hon. gentleman called attention to the fact that it was six o'clock, and the Speaker said. "I am in the hands of the house," and put the question whether he should leave the chair or not.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a positive rule in this case. It is a new rule, standing order 7, which says:
At eleven of the clock, p.m., unless the closure rule standing order No. 39 be then in operation, the proceedings on any business under consideration shall be interrupted and Mr. Speaker shall adjourn the house without question put.
I have asked if it be the unanimous wish of the house that we proceed, and I am told that there is not unanimous consent.
